TEXT:
Surfers Paradise, Gold Coast >$3.3 million

Andrew MacDonald, senior

vice-president and chief casino officer at Singapore's Marina Bay Sands, is selling his penthouse in the Mantra Chevron Renaissance Towers. Offering views of the city skyline, ocean and hinterland, the three-bedroom apartment comes with an 80-square-metre living room, three bathrooms, three balconies, parking and

a heated rooftop plunge pool. Each of the three bedrooms has an en suite, the master with a bath enjoying the ocean views.

Kerry-Jayne Broad of Queensland Sotheby's International has the listing.

Malvern, Adelaide $3.5 million

Reena Costello, a solicitor with New York construction law firm Zetlin & De Chiara, has listed her circa 1919 triple-fronted bungalow, set on 2290 square metres in one of the suburb's best streets. The four-bedroom, three-bathroom home has adjoining formal living and dining rooms, a conservatory, family meals area and a Miele kitchen with twin pantries. Outside, there is a selection of entertaining areas, a pool and a tennis court. The property goes to auction on April 8 with Stephanie Williams of Harcourts Williams Luxury.

Wellington Point, Brisbane Auction

Sherrin Group managing director and racing car driver Michael Sherrin is selling his character home in tightly held Champion Lane. One of only a handful

of properties facing north over Moreton Bay, the home is set over three blocks totalling 1280 square metres. The

two-bedroom, two-bathroom property comes with a modern kitchen, a wraparound verandah, a double garage and a pool. McGrath Bulimba agent Glen Bool, who sold the neighbouring property two years ago for $1.7 million, will take the property to auction on April 9.

HEADLINE: City slicker
TEXT:
Melbourne CBD $2.75 million

Barrister John Salamanca is selling his two-storey apartment in the Republic Tower on Queen Street. Designed by Nonda Katsilidis, the building has a rooftop pool and communal gymnasium. The three-bedroom apartment has a stone and gas kitchen, a fitted study, an upper-level master retreat, a mezzanine dining room and a balcony wrapping around the living room. The property is listed for sale with Anton Wongtrakun of Dingle Partners.

South Fremantle, Perth $1.5 million

Retired property manager Marilyn Hawkins and her husband, Laurie, have listed their 1890s limestone cottage. Designed by architect Norman Hitchcock, who was known for his overtly decorative style, the four-bedroom home retains period features, including a bull-nosed verandah, original fireplaces, decorative plasterwork and high ceilings. There's also a granny flat and workshop in established gardens.

The property is for sale through Mark Brophy of Mark Brophy Estate Agents South Fremantle.

HEADLINE: The ethnic threat to free speech
TEXT:
Ethnic groups with political clout that import old grievances and a collectivist mentality threaten Australian liberal values.

When Labor, the Greens and certain Liberals in western Sydney seats seek to explain their reasons for opposing changes to section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act, they mostly refer to the concerns of ethnic, religious and racial minority groups.

Representatives of Armenian, Hellenic, Indian, Chinese and Vietnamese groups have joined Jewish, Lebanese Muslim and Arab groups to oppose any changes apart from procedural, arguing that amending section 18C will unleash a torrent of "hate speech".

While we occasionally hear half-hearted claims that minorities require special protection from hurt feelings, the main driver of opposition is the political clout of these groups. A dozen or so federal seats are held on margins smaller than the populations of these groups. And in the recent state election in Western Australia, certain Muslim leaders openly endorsed the Greens.

The debate over S18C is much greater than free speech. It is, in fact, a fight for the votes of people who have different values from those of traditional Australia. Instead of embracing the values of their adopted country, these ethnic, religious and immigrant representatives want Australia to become more like the countries they left behind.

Australia has a deeply rooted tradition of freedom in which free speech is central. Our legal and cultural origins lie in Britain, where the primacy of individuals over collectivism first took root. The same values led the US to make free speech the first amendment in its Bill of Rights.

Australia has been a leading supporter of free speech internationally. It was a founding member of the United Nations under the leadership of former Labor minister Dr Herbert Vere Evatt, who became president of the UN General Assembly and was instrumental in drafting and having adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Article 19 of the declaration states: "Everyone has the right to freedom of opinion and expression; this right includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media and regardless of frontiers."

Freedom of association, worship and movement, freedom from arbitrary arrest, equality before the law and free speech are generally regarded as the bedrock of a free society. On top of these, Australia has embraced equality and respect, irrespective of gender or personal attributes, and rejected claims of inherited status and class.

These values are not necessarily shared by those who come to Australia. Certain Armenians accuse Turkey of genocide but want to suppress its response; Greeks can have issues with Turks and Macedonians; Indians can be racist when it comes to West Indian cricketers but are sensitive to the same speech themselves; those from Arabic and Lebanese Muslim cultures can hold abhorrent views about women and gays, and resolve matters of feelings and honour through violence; and many Jews want to suppress Holocaust denialism.

After World War II, immigrants who arrived in Australia either abandoned their historic grievances or chose not to share them with others. Millions of post-war immigrants from dozens of countries integrated, assimilated and did their best to become true-blue Aussies. For their part, Australians welcomed these immigrants as "New Australians" and embraced their food, music and dance.

The fact that leaders of immigrant, ethnic and religious groups are now flexing their political muscle in pursuit of different values is a major concern. Not only does it threaten traditional liberal values, it fuels opposition to immigration among the community and gives credence to demands to block certain types of immigrants.

Australia cannot afford this; its economic growth depends on a substantial flow of skilled immigrants. (Family reunion immigrants are less beneficial.) It would cost us dearly if we were to close our borders to the talents and expertise that immigration delivers.

Other countries have addressed this problem by raising the bar on citizenship. Switzerland, for example, has a relatively relaxed attitude to immigrants provided they find a job. However, becoming a Swiss citizen and eligible to vote in elections requires 10 years of residence, no criminal record, a solid employment history and endorsement by the applicant's canton. In practical terms, unless they have embraced "Swiss values", they do not become citizens.

Opposition to changes to 18C is a wake-up call. Australia's traditional liberal values are under siege like never before. With one side of politics already in full retreat, it is vital the other side steps up to protect those values before it is too late.

HEADLINE: The Liveris lesson on Donald Trump
TEXT:
After Rupert Murdoch, Andrew Liveris is one of Australia's most prominent global business figures. The head of Dow Chemical also has spent more time with President Donald Trump than any other Australian. From never having met the new president, Darwin-born Mr Liveris has become one of the new president's chief corporate advisers on reviving US manufacturing, partly on the strength of his 2011 book 'Make it in America'. As exclusively reported by Jennifer Hewett on page one of The Australian Financial Review yesterday, Mr Liveris provides one of the most informed interpretations of the new president's economic and business agenda.

The Liveris interpretation mostly sidesteps Mr Trump's trade protectionism and his harsh anti-immigration posture. These are as distasteful to the American multinationals that have driven globalisation as they are against the interests of a commodity-exporting immigrant society such as Australia's. For Mr Trump, however, companies such as Dow Chemical are icons of the golden era of American industry. Mr Trump and Mr Liveris clearly agree on the scope to revive American manufacturing by cutting back the red and green tape regulation piled high by the business-blind Obama administration. They agree on reskilling the American workforce for the information age economy - new collar workers rather than the old blue collar toilers. Mr Liveris backs Mr Trump's plans for Reaganite tax cuts and deregulation along with infrastructure spending on the scale of Franklin Roosevelt. And he can appreciate Mr Trump's plans to make America less of a consumer society and more of a nation of investors, producers and exporters. That's the idea behind Mr Trump's planned personal and company income tax cuts. His mooted border adjustment tax sounds too protectionist. But the possible alternative of a value added tax would shift the tax burden from income to consumption - as we need to do.

Mr Liveris accommodates Mr Trump's populism by arguing that America's financial capitalism enriched the "very, very 1 per cent" while hurting an American working class already suffering from unfair globalisation. Here he even sounds like the ACTU's Sally McManus, ironic as Mr Trump's economic agenda being crafted by former Goldman Sachs bankers.

As Mr Liveris points out, America is already being buoyed by gas developments that Australia has stupidly refused to recreate. But the wider point is that the protectionist and anti-wealth creator populism simply do not apply here. Australia didn't have an oversized casino banking sector. We were saved from the global GFC recession by China's stimulus spending on our iron ore and coal. We've controlled our borders. Australia's speculator class comprises suburbanites out-bidding each other at house auctions. Unlike the US, Australia doesn't have the muscle to push around China or European for better trade deals. We can only compete on our merits. That means we need to fix our energy mess, our tax system and our workplace regulation. That would generate economic growth, and as Mr Liveris puts it for both countries: "growth forgives many sins".

American graffiti

The United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney was set up with $25 million of Howard government money to balance out the anti-American bias on Australian campuses. As Aaron Patrick reported in The Australian Financial Review yesterday, the centre has instead demonstrated Australian academia's default setting of veering off to the cultural left. Its research on US policy is excellent, and frequently appears on these pages. Its teaching on US culture can descend into post-modernist glop. For example: "The layered frameworks of film history and theory, queer theory, and transnationalism structure the counter-intuitive intervention of using the image to read novels, and novels to historicise the image". Did we need to know this about the US? Could we even tell? This is a waste of resources in what should be the productive and useful enterprise of scrutinising our most important global relationship.

HEADLINE: Way down in Kokomo
TEXT: Lang Walker went to Sydney's Jannali High School, then quit accounting studies to join his father's earth moving business in the 1960s. Today, he is Australia's 17th richest person with a multibillion-dollar property empire. But the project that really tested him was Kokomo Island in Fiji, the first resort he's built and managed. Walker has left no stone unturned to ensure it makes a splash when it opens next month, writes Fiona Carruthers. AFR Magazine The Fashion Issue | Inside

HEADLINE: Fair Work row rocks leave case
TEXT:
A landmark Fair Work Commission case for establishing a new legal right for workers to 10 days' paid domestic violence leave a year is in turmoil after a rejection of the ACTU's claim by the full bench's senior member has been thrown into doubt.

In an extraordinary internal dispute, the retired head of the domestic violence full bench, vice-president Graeme Watson last night accused his colleagues, one in favour of the leave and the other undecided before taking sick leave, of making false claims against him.

The intervention follows the announcement on Monday by FWC president Iain Ross that he was considering reconstituting the full bench on the delayed case, which would effectively render Mr Watson's early rejection of the claim "null and void".

Employer groups viewed Mr Watson's decision, handed down on the eve of his retirement on February 28 and before the two other bench members had reached a decision, as a major setback for the union movement's claim, which they estimate will cost business an additional $205 million a year.

However, Justice Ross this week disclosed an internal memorandum from the other members, deputy president Anne Gooley and commissioner Paula Spencer, alleging Mr Watson had refused to share his conclusion with them before publishing it.

The members said Mr Watson had only sent them a draft of his decision on February 20 after repeated requests and claimed it did not include his final conclusion. There was not enough time to then consider the draft and release their own decision, they said.

They questioned whether they could now issue decisions separately that would still constitute "a full bench" or whether the president would need to appoint a new member to the bench.

Mr Watson hit back at those claims on Wednesday in a statement sent to employer groups and unions, obtained by The Australian Financial Review, saying that the memorandum was "misleading" and "not a complete and accurate statement".

Mr Watson said neither Justice Ross nor the other members had contacted him about the matter.

"The publication of those allegations about internal communications, their inaccuracy and the environment at the time when normal professional courtesies were not being observed, has led me to issue this statement."

Contrary to claims he had not shared his final conclusion, Mr Watson said he had advised his colleagues as early as after final hearings on December 2 that he would refuse the domestic violence leave claim. The former vice-president also revealed the bench was split on the matter, with Ms Gooley saying she "disagreed with my views" and Ms Spencer "undecided".

Despite advising them in early February that he was close to finalising his reasons by February 10, Mr Watson said both indicated they were not ready to hand down a decision.

The deadline for Fair Work decisions is for 90 per cent to be handed down within two months of final hearing and 100 per cent within three months, meaning the end of February was the latest date.

Mr Watson said Ms Spencer was still undecided as at February 20 and he formed the view she was "confused about my views and of the protocols for preparing decisions by full bench members".

In an email to his colleagues that day, he said: "I do not wish to provide my reasons for saying no to the claim and have my reasons criticised in a decision deciding to grant the claim. This has happened before and I regard it as unethical."

However, "to resolve the impasse", he sent them his latest draft, including his conclusion that he was not satisfied the unions' claim for domestic violence leave was necessary to provide a "fair and relevant safety net".

Commissioner Spencer later told him on February 24 she had been advised to take a week's sick leave, effective immediately.

Mr Watson's published decision refused the unions' claim due to its "uncertain consequences" and because awareness campaigns would better encourage a collaborative approach with employers.

"If employees seek to take paid leave for purposes which are regarded as having a tenuous link with actual physical violence, the entitlement may lead to a deterioration in workplace relationships."

His only substantive change to his draft was to mention that the majority position would be determined after his published decision, which he said was an "entirely conventional" statement, although uncommon given the "unusual" circumstances.

Parties to the domestic violence case must make submissions by April 4 on whether a new member should now be appointed.
